title: Context windows
scopeHtml: What the context window is and what limits it, position extrapolation, lost-in-the-middle, effective vs advertised context, long context vs RAG, context rot, cost/latency of long prompts, and context management. Numbers for specific models are illustrative or marked "verify".

questions.promptHtml: What is a context window, and what actually limits how large it can be?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you see the window as a hard architectural and memory constraint, not just a number on a pricing page.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can attend to in one forward pass: prompt plus everything it generates. It is limited by three things: the length the model was trained at (positions beyond that are unfamiliar), the O(n^2) attention compute, and the KV-cache memory that grows linearly with tokens. A provider's advertised number is where those three were engineered to hold up, not a guarantee of quality.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A transformer has no memory between calls. Every request re-feeds the whole conversation as tokens, and the model attends over all of them. The window is therefore the model's entire working memory.

Three independent limits:

  1. Training length. Position information (e.g. RoPE rotation angles) is only seen up to some length during training. Beyond it the model sees angles it never learned, and quality collapses (see Q130/Q131).
  2. Compute. Self-attention scores are an n x n matrix per head: doubling the prompt quadruples prefill attention work. FlashAttention removes the n x n memory materialization but not the FLOPs.
  3. Memory. Each token's keys and values are cached for every layer; this is linear in n but large (Q127). It caps concurrent users per GPU long before compute does.
 [ system | history ... | retrieved docs | user msg |  <- output tokens ->  ]
 |<------------------------- context window --------------------------->|

Input and output share the same window. A 128K window with a 120K prompt leaves about 8K for the answer (providers also set a separate max-output cap).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import tiktoken
enc = tiktoken.get_encoding("o200k_base")  # use the tokenizer of YOUR model
def fits(prompt: str, window: int, reserve_output: int) -> bool:
    return len(enc.encode(prompt)) + reserve_output <= window

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating the window as input-only and forgetting output (and reasoning tokens) consume it.
  • Counting characters or words instead of the model's own tokens.
  • Assuming "supports 1M" means "answers well at 1M".

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why doesn't the model just remember the previous turn? → Stateless; the client resends history, which is why chat cost grows with each turn.
  2. Is the limit a property of the architecture or of the weights? → Mostly weights/training; RoPE has no hard max, but quality outside trained lengths is not guaranteed.
  3. Which limit bites first in serving? → Usually KV memory (batch size drops), then prefill latency.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "max tokens it can read". The senior names the three limits, knows input and output share it, and connects it to serving capacity and cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team sized for 8K prompts moved to 64K RAG contexts and found the same GPUs served a fraction of the concurrency because KV cache, not weights, filled memory.

questions.subtopic: Token budgeting across input and output
questions.promptHtml: How do you budget a context window between system prompt, history, retrieved content and the model's answer?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests practical discipline: reserving output space and having a deterministic policy for what gets cut.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I compute the budget as window minus reserved output, then allocate fixed shares: system prompt and tools are non-negotiable, the latest user message is non-negotiable, and history and retrieval fill the rest by priority. I count with the model's real tokenizer, keep a safety margin for template overhead, and decide up front what is trimmed first so overflow never becomes a runtime error.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Example, 32K window: output reserve 2K, system+tools 1.5K, current user turn 0.5K, safety margin 3% (about 1K) for chat-template tokens. Remaining about 27K is shared: say 8K recent history, 19K retrieval. If history exceeds 8K, summarize oldest turns; if retrieval exceeds 19K, drop lowest-ranked chunks, never truncate mid-chunk.

Rules of thumb:

  • Reserve output first. Reasoning models can spend thousands of hidden tokens (verify per provider) that count against the window.
  • Template overhead (role markers, tool schemas) is not in your raw text count. Count the rendered message list, not the strings.
  • Put a hard assertion before the API call; failing fast beats a provider 400 error or silent truncation.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def build(system, history, docs, user, count, window=32_000, out=2_000):
    budget = window - out - count(system) - count(user) - int(0.03 * window)
    kept_hist, kept_docs = [], []
    hist_cap = min(8_000, budget // 3)
    for m in reversed(history):                 # newest first
        if count(m) > hist_cap: break
        kept_hist.insert(0, m); hist_cap -= count(m)
    left = budget - sum(count(m) for m in kept_hist)
    for d in docs:                              # docs already ranked
        if count(d) > left: break
        kept_docs.append(d); left -= count(d)
    return kept_hist, kept_docs

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Budgeting only input; the model then gets cut off mid-answer.
  • Truncating from the front, which removes the system prompt.
  • Using a different tokenizer than the target model (see the tokenization chunk).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What do you cut first? → Oldest history turns (summarize), then low-rank retrieval; never system or current turn.
  2. How do you handle tool outputs of unknown size? → Cap each tool result and return a truncated view with a pointer to fetch more.
  3. How do you validate it? → Property test with random lengths asserting total <= window for every input.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "trim the history". Senior: explicit priority tiers, output reserve, counted-with-template, invariants tested, and telemetry on how often each tier is cut.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An agent that appended unbounded tool output hit context overflow on 3% of sessions; capping each tool result at 2K tokens cut the errors to near zero.

questions.promptHtml: Estimate the KV-cache memory for a 128K-token request on a Llama-3-8B-class model. Why does it matter for long context?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who can size infrastructure from those who only call APIs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Per token the cache stores K and V for every layer: 2 x layers x KV heads x head_dim x bytes. For an 8B model with 32 layers, 8 KV heads (GQA), head_dim 128 in bf16, that is 131,072 bytes, 128 KiB per token. At 128K tokens that is about 16 GiB for one request, as much as the model weights themselves. So concurrency collapses as context grows.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Formula: bytes_per_token = 2 * n_layers * n_kv_heads * head_dim * dtype_bytes.

  • 8B-class (verify config): 2 x 32 x 8 x 128 x 2 = 131,072 B.
  • 128K tokens = 131,072 tokens -> 131,072 x 131,072 B = 17.2e9 B, about 16 GiB.
  • A 70B-class model (80 layers, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128, verify): 2 x 80 x 8 x 128 x 2 = 327,680 B/token; at 128K about 40 GiB per request.
  • Without GQA (64 KV heads instead of 8) the 8B number would be 8x larger.

On an 80 GB GPU holding 16 GB of bf16 8B weights, about 60 GB remains for cache after overhead: roughly 3 concurrent 128K requests, versus about 60 at 8K contexts. Mitigations: GQA/MQA, KV quantization to fp8/int8 (halves it, small quality cost), PagedAttention to avoid fragmentation, prefix sharing, sliding-window layers, cache offload. Deep serving treatment belongs to C2.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def kv_bytes(tokens, layers=32, kv_heads=8, head_dim=128, dtype_bytes=2):
    return 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * dtype_bytes * tokens

print(kv_bytes(131_072) / 2**30)   # ~16.0 GiB

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using attention heads instead of KV heads (overestimates 4-8x on GQA models).
  • Forgetting the leading 2 (K and V).
  • Forgetting this is per sequence, so it multiplies by batch size.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does fp8 KV do? → Halves bytes, so 8 GiB at 128K; check long-context quality on your eval.
  2. Does cache grow during decoding? → Yes, one token's worth per generated token.
  3. Why does prefix caching help? → Shared prefix blocks are stored once and reused across requests.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "it uses a lot of memory". The senior gives the formula, the GQA effect, the concurrency consequence and the mitigation menu.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A self-hosted deployment passed load tests at 4K and OOMed in prod when users pasted 100K-token documents; admission control by estimated KV bytes fixed it.

questions.subtopic: Prefill vs decode cost of long prompts
questions.promptHtml: Why does a long prompt make the first token slow, while later tokens are less affected? What is the real cost scaling?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests understanding of the two inference phases and which costs are quadratic.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Prefill processes all n prompt tokens in parallel; its attention work scales as n^2 and its linear-layer work as n, so time to first token (TTFT) grows super-linearly with prompt length. Decode generates one token at a time, attending to the cached n keys, so each step costs O(n) memory reads but is dominated by reading weights and cache from memory. Long prompts hurt TTFT a lot and per-token speed modestly.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Prefill FLOPs roughly: 2 * params * n (matmuls) plus attention ~ 4 * layers * d_model * n^2. For short n the first term dominates; once n is tens of thousands the n^2 term takes over. For a 7-8B model, the crossover is at roughly n near 16 x d_model scale (about tens of K tokens); treat as order-of-magnitude.

Decode is memory-bandwidth bound: each step reads all weights plus the whole KV cache. A 16 GiB cache on a GPU with about 2-3 TB/s bandwidth adds roughly 5-8 ms per token on top of weight reads (illustrative; verify hardware).

FlashAttention (Dao et al.) tiles the computation so the n x n matrix never lives in HBM. It cuts memory and wall-clock, but total FLOPs are still quadratic.

Provider-side: input tokens are billed per 1M, and long prompts are also slower to start, so cost and latency both scale with prompt size. Chunked prefill interleaves prefill with decode so one huge prompt does not stall others.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying decode is quadratic; per step it is linear in cache length.
  • Claiming FlashAttention makes attention linear.
  • Ignoring that TTFT, not total time, is what users feel in chat.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you cut TTFT for a repeated 50K system context? → Prefix/prompt caching.
  2. Why batch prefill and decode differently? → Prefill is compute-bound, decode memory-bound.
  3. What does sliding-window attention change? → Attention per token is bounded by window w, making cost O(n*w).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "longer prompts are slower". Senior: separates compute-bound prefill from memory-bound decode, locates the n^2 term, and proposes caching and chunked prefill.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A summarization feature had p50 TTFT of 0.8 s at 4K and 9 s at 60K; moving the static instructions and corpus into a cached prefix cut it sharply.

questions.contextHtml: A support copilot sends, per request, a 6K-token system prompt (policies, tool schemas, 40 few-shot examples), plus 2K of conversation and a 500-token answer. Traffic is 2M requests/day. Illustrative pricing: $3 per 1M input tokens, $15 per 1M output tokens (verify your provider; cached input is typically discounted). Monthly bill is about $1.4M and finance wants it down 40%. p95 TTFT is 3.2 s. Someone proposes switching to a smaller model.
questions.promptHtml: How do you cut cost and latency without hurting quality?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use a cheaper model" or "shorten the prompt" without measuring. It skips that 75% of input is a static prefix, ignores caching, and never checks quality impact.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What share of the 6K prefix is identical across requests (is it byte-identical)? Is quality measured by an eval set? Are few-shots all needed? What is the latency SLO? Does the provider offer prompt caching and what is the TTL?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ensure the static prefix comes first and is byte-identical; enable provider prompt caching. No quality risk.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) static prefix is 6K of 8.5K input, so caching hits the largest cost; (b) 40 few-shots include redundant ones; (c) history is resent in full and could be summarized; (d) output length is verbose; (e) model is oversized for easy intents.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compute per-request token breakdown from logs. Daily input: 2M x 8K = 16B tokens -> $48K/day input; output 2M x 500 = 1B -> $15K/day. Input is about 76% of spend. If 6K of 8K is cached at, say, 10% of price (verify), input drops to roughly 2M x (6K x 0.1 + 2K) x $3/1M = $15.6K/day. Run ablation of few-shot count on the eval set; sample-based check for model downgrade.
  5. Root cause: Pay-per-token on a prefix that never changes, recomputed each request.
  6. Fix: Short term: caching, stable prefix ordering, no timestamps or user IDs in the prefix (they break the cache). Medium term: prune few-shots to the 8-10 that move eval scores, dynamic few-shot selection, history summarization, route easy intents to a small model.
  7. Prevention: Dashboard for cache hit rate, tokens per request by section, cost per resolved ticket; CI test that fails if the prefix hash changes unexpectedly.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not swap the model first (quality risk, retraining of prompts). Not cache with long TTL on policies that change daily without invalidation. Caching helps latency only on hits.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Cache hit rate is only 20%, why? -> Dynamic content early in the prompt or multiple prefix variants; reorder and normalise.
  • Provider has no caching? -> Self-host with prefix caching, or shrink the prefix by fine-tuning behaviour in (C6).
  • Quality drops after pruning few-shots on one intent? -> Per-intent eval, keep examples for that intent only.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team found a timestamp at the top of the system prompt defeating caching for months; moving it to the end of the user turn cut input spend by more than half.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests only a cheaper model or vague compression.
  • Hire: identifies static prefix, uses caching, does the token math.
  • Strong hire: also covers cache-breaking pitfalls, per-intent evals, routing, and monitoring of cache hit rate.

questions.promptHtml: Why does a model trained on 4K tokens fall apart when you feed it 16K, even though nothing in the architecture forbids it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Probes understanding of positional encodings as the real source of the training-length limit.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Attention itself accepts any length, but the position signal does not. With RoPE, each token's query and key are rotated by an angle proportional to position; beyond the trained range the model sees rotation angles and relative distances it never saw, so attention scores become unpredictable. Perplexity explodes. The fix is to remap positions into the trained range or retrain a little at the longer length.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
RoPE rotates each pair of dimensions i by pos * theta_i, with theta_i = base^(-2i/d) (base 10000 in the original RoFormer; many newer models use larger bases, verify per model). The dot product of rotated q and k depends on relative distance m - n. Low-frequency dimensions (small theta) rotate slowly and never wrap within 4K; high-frequency dimensions wrap many times and are seen at many phases.

At 16K, relative distances up to 16K appear. The low-frequency dimensions now take phase values outside anything seen in training; the model's learned attention patterns misfire. The Position Interpolation paper reports that extrapolation can produce catastrophically high attention scores.

trained:  distances 0 ............ 4K
test:     distances 0 ............ 4K .......... 16K  <- never seen

Other schemes fail differently: learned absolute embeddings have no row beyond max length; sinusoidal degrade; ALiBi extrapolates better by design (linear distance penalty) but still weakens.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "attention is O(n^2) so it can't".
  • Believing the limit is a config flag you can just raise (max_position_embeddings).
  • Assuming perplexity staying finite means long-range retrieval works.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does ALiBi extrapolate better? → Bias is a fixed function of distance, not a learned/rotated signal.
  2. Which RoPE dimensions are the problem? → Low-frequency ones, whose full phase range was never covered.
  3. Does raising the rope base help? → Yes, it stretches wavelengths; see Q131.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "it wasn't trained that long". Senior pinpoints RoPE phase/out-of-distribution distances and distinguishes perplexity from retrieval.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team bumped the max length of an open model's config and saw fluent but nonsensical output past the trained length, with no error raised.

questions.promptHtml: Explain how Position Interpolation, NTK-aware scaling and YaRN extend a RoPE model's context, and what you give up with each.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Senior-level knowledge of how open models get 32K-128K windows after pretraining.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Position Interpolation divides positions by a scale factor s so longer inputs map into the trained range; it needs a short fine-tune and blurs local resolution. NTK-aware scaling changes the RoPE base instead, stretching low frequencies a lot and high frequencies little, so nearby tokens stay distinguishable. YaRN combines per-frequency interpolation with an attention temperature tweak and needs much less fine-tuning data. All trade some short-context sharpness for reach.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• PI (Chen et al. 2023): pos' = pos / s, e.g. s=8 maps 32K onto 4K. All frequencies are compressed equally, so adjacent tokens get closer in angle and become harder to separate. The paper reports extending LLaMA to 32K with fine-tuning within about 1000 steps and a much smaller extrapolation bound than naive extrapolation.
  • NTK-aware: Rescale base: base' = base * s^(d/(d-2)). High-frequency dims barely change; low-frequency dims interpolate. Works zero-shot to a degree, community-developed (verify exact derivation in source).
  • YaRN (Peng et al. 2023): Splits dimensions by wavelength relative to the trained length: no interpolation for high-frequency, full interpolation for low-frequency, a ramp in between ("NTK-by-parts"), and a temperature on attention logits to counter entropy shift. Authors report needing about 10x fewer tokens and 2.5x fewer steps than prior methods (from abstract; implementation constants: verify in paper).

Rule: any extension past training length is validated on your task, not only on perplexity. Also dynamic variants adjust scale per actual input length so short inputs are unaffected.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
# Hugging Face config style (verify keys for your model/version)
from transformers import AutoConfig
cfg = AutoConfig.from_pretrained("meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B")
cfg.rope_scaling = {"rope_type": "yarn", "factor": 4.0,
                    "original_max_position_embeddings": 8192}
cfg.max_position_embeddings = 32768

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Applying a fixed scale at inference to all lengths, degrading short prompts (use dynamic scaling or only when needed).
  • Evaluating only perplexity or needle tests after extension.
  • Forgetting that serving stacks must implement the same scaling as training.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does PI hurt local precision? → Positions are squeezed, so neighbours differ by 1/s of an angle step.
  2. How much data to fine-tune? → PI: ~1000 steps reported; YaRN: fewer tokens; domain data helps.
  3. Is a larger rope base at pretraining better? → Many long-context models pretrain or continue-pretrain with larger bases; verify per model card.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "they stretch the positions". Senior contrasts uniform vs per-frequency scaling, names the short-context cost, and insists on task-level validation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An inference engine applied a different rope scaling than the checkpoint was tuned with and long-document accuracy dropped silently; a config parity test caught the next one.

questions.promptHtml: What is the "lost in the middle" effect, and how does it change how you assemble prompts?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A well-known empirical result that directly affects RAG prompt layout.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Liu et al. found that models answer best when the relevant information is at the start or end of the context and worse when it is in the middle, a U-shaped accuracy curve, even for models built for long inputs. In practice I put the most important instructions and evidence at the edges, keep context short, rerank so top results are first, and measure position sensitivity on my own data because newer models vary.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Setup in the paper: multi-document QA where the answer-bearing document is moved among k documents, and a synthetic key-value retrieval task. Accuracy depended on position, with primacy and recency effects. Plausible causes (hypotheses, not proven): attention sinks and bias toward early tokens, recency from the causal training objective, and training data where relevant info often sits at the boundaries.

Practical layout:

[ system instructions ]
[ most relevant doc ]  <- start
[ weaker docs ... ]    <- middle
[ second most relevant ]  <- end
[ question restated ]

Restating the question at the end, and putting a long document before the question (not after) are common provider recommendations (verify per provider docs).

The effect size changes by model and generation; recent models show a flatter curve on simple retrieval, but multi-fact or reasoning tasks still show sensitivity. Never assume it is gone.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Sorting retrieved chunks by document order rather than relevance.
  • Believing bigger window removes the effect.
  • Testing only with a single easy needle.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you test it on your own system? → Hold the gold chunk fixed, sweep its position, plot accuracy.
  2. Does reranking help? → Yes: fewer, better chunks and good ordering reduce reliance on the middle.
  3. Does it apply to output? → Different issue; instruction-following over long output is tested separately.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "put important stuff at the start". Senior: edges layout, empirical position sweep, and treat it as model-specific rather than a law.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A RAG bot's accuracy rose several points just from reordering top-k so rank 1 and rank 2 sat at both ends.

questions.promptHtml: What does a needle-in-a-haystack test measure, and why can a model ace it and still fail on your documents?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests skepticism about vendor long-context claims.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The test hides one fact in a long filler text and asks the model to retrieve it, sweeping length and depth. It measures literal lookup of a distinctive string. Models that score near 100% can still fail at multi-fact aggregation, reasoning across the text, or when the needle looks like surrounding content. So I use it as a smoke test, then run RULER-style or task-specific evals.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Why it is easy: the needle (e.g. "the secret code is 7421") stands out semantically from the filler, so attention can latch onto the odd one out. Real documents have many similar passages, near-duplicates and conflicts.

RULER (Hsieh et al.) extends it with multiple needles, multi-hop tracing and aggregation tasks; the authors report that nearly all models score near-perfect on vanilla NIAH yet degrade with length on the harder tasks, and only about half of 17 models claiming 32K+ stayed satisfactory at 32K.

Build your own test: take real documents, plant realistic facts that mirror the question types you serve, include distractors similar to the needle, sweep length x position, report accuracy heatmaps with confidence intervals.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import random
def make_case(filler_docs, fact, question, depth, n_tokens, count):
    text, i = [], 0
    while count(" ".join(text)) < n_tokens:
        text.append(filler_docs[i % len(filler_docs)]); i += 1
    text.insert(int(len(text) * depth), fact)
    return " ".join(text) + f"\n\nQuestion: {question}"

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using random-word filler and a goofy needle, then declaring victory.
  • Single trial per cell (noisy).
  • Treating a pass as evidence of reasoning ability.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does multi-needle show? → Retrieval and recall drop as count rises.
  2. What about aggregation tasks? → Counting or summing across the text exposes weaker effective length.
  3. Can the test be contaminated? → Yes, famous needles can be memorized; use fresh facts.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "it shows if the model finds info". Senior: knows its limits, RULER, and builds domain-realistic variants.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A vendor demo showed green heatmaps; the buyer's own contract-clause test with similar clauses showed mid-length failures.

questions.contextHtml:
A chat service trims history to fit a 16K window. Users report that after long conversations the assistant "forgets its rules" and sometimes returns a provider 400 context_length_exceeded (prompt 16,412 tokens > 16,384). Average conversation is 40 turns; system prompt is 1.2K tokens; max output is set to 1,024. Code:

def trim(messages, count, limit=16384):
    total = sum(count(m["content"]) for m in messages)
    while total > limit and len(messages) > 1:
        removed = messages.pop(0)
        total -= count(removed["content"])
    return messages

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Just lower the limit a bit." Misses that the system message is popped first, that output is not reserved, and that message-format overhead is uncounted.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which tokenizer does count use (same as the model)? Is the system prompt the first element of messages? Are there tool messages? Does the provider count per-message overhead? Is max_tokens set?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pin the system message, reserve output, lower limit by a margin as a hotfix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) pop(0) drops the system message first, explaining "forgets rules"; (b) limit equals the window, but 1,024 output tokens are needed, so prompt must be <= 15,360; (c) per-message template overhead (a few tokens per message x 40 turns) is uncounted, explaining the 16,412 vs counted lower total; (d) mutates the caller's list in place; (e) count uses a different tokenizer (red herring unless confirmed).
  4. How I'd verify each: Log the first role after trimming; compare local count vs provider usage.prompt_tokens on the same payload to measure overhead; unit test with a 60-turn fixture.
  5. Root cause: Window arithmetic ignores output reserve and format overhead, and trimming is position-based rather than role-aware.
  6. Fix:
def trim(messages, count, window=16384, out=1024, per_msg=4, margin=200):
    sys_msgs = [m for m in messages if m["role"] == "system"]
    rest = [m for m in messages if m["role"] != "system"]
    cost = lambda m: count(m["content"]) + per_msg
    budget = window - out - margin - sum(cost(m) for m in sys_msgs)
    kept = []
    for m in reversed(rest):                 # keep newest
        if cost(m) > budget: break
        kept.insert(0, m); budget -= cost(m)
    return sys_msgs + kept

Long term: summarize dropped turns, and reconcile local count against usage from responses. 7. Prevention: Property test: result tokens + out <= window for random inputs; alert on 400 context errors; log estimate-vs-actual drift. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not rely on a magic margin only; not drop assistant/tool pairs separately (breaks tool-call validity); summarization costs an extra call.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The newest single message exceeds the budget? -> Reject or truncate that message with explicit notice; never silently drop it.
  • Tool-call message pairs? -> Drop as atomic units.
  • Different tokenizer used by count? -> Use the model's own tokenizer or a provider token-count endpoint (verify availability).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A support bot "went rogue" in long chats; the oldest-first trim had been deleting the safety instructions at turn 30.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: lowers limit only.
  • Hire: pins system, reserves output.
  • Strong hire: also overhead, atomic tool pairs, tests and drift telemetry.

questions.contextHtml: A product manager says: "The vendor's model has a 1M-token window, so we'll let customers upload their whole knowledge base (up to 700K tokens) and ask questions. No RAG needed." Questions are mixed: lookups ("what is the refund window?") and cross-document ones ("which of our policies conflict with the new EU rule?"). Target: 90% answer accuracy, p95 latency under 20 s, about 5K queries/day. Illustrative price $2.50 per 1M input tokens (verify). No eval set exists yet.
questions.promptHtml: How do you respond and what do you do next?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Sure, 700K fits in 1M, ship it." Equates window size with usable capacity and never prices or evaluates it.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How often does the knowledge base change? What share of questions are lookup vs cross-document? Is the 90% measured on what? Is the same KB reused across many queries (cache-friendly) or per-customer one-offs? What are the data residency limits?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I would build a 100-question eval set from real questions before committing to an architecture.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) advertised window is not effective window: accuracy degrades with length and task complexity (RULER-style findings); (b) cost: 700K x 5K queries = 3.5B tokens/day = $8,750/day uncached; (c) latency: prefill of 700K tokens will not meet 20 s likely; (d) cross-document questions may still need long context, so a hybrid is plausible.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run the eval at 50K, 200K and 700K context with the same questions; plot accuracy vs length by question type; measure TTFT; compute cost with and without prompt caching (cache discount and TTL: verify).
  5. Root cause of the risk: Confusing capacity (fits) with capability (uses it reliably).
  6. Fix: Propose a staged design: retrieval to 20-50K relevant tokens for lookups; long-context mode only for cross-document questions over a cached, curated subset. Decide with data.
  7. Prevention: Keep the long-context eval in CI per model upgrade; monitor accuracy by input length in production.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not reject long context outright (it simplifies pipelines for static corpora); not commit before eval; do not promise 90% without a measured baseline.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The eval shows 88% at 700K and 91% at 50K retrieved? -> Hybrid wins on cost and accuracy; long context only as fallback.
  • KB is only 150K tokens and static? -> Cached long-context may beat RAG on simplicity; cost check.
  • Vendor releases a new model next month? -> Re-run the same eval; do not re-architect on a press release.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team launched "whole-corpus" Q&A on a headline window size; accuracy on multi-hop questions was about 20 points below single-fact ones, and the bill was 12x the estimate.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: accepts the window as capacity.
  • Hire: asks for evals, notes cost and latency.
  • Strong hire: segments by question type, computes numbers, proposes hybrid with CI regression.

questions.promptHtml: When would you choose long-context prompting over RAG, and when the reverse? Isn't RAG dead now?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Core architecture judgment: can you reason across cost, accuracy, freshness and governance rather than repeat a slogan.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: They solve different constraints. Long context wins when the corpus is small enough to fit and cache, the task needs holistic or cross-document reasoning, and I want fewer moving parts. RAG wins when the corpus is much larger than any window, changes often, needs access control or citations, or when per-query cost and latency matter. Most production systems end up hybrid: retrieve broadly, then give the model a generous but curated context.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Dimension Long context RAG
Corpus size Must fit (and quality drops near the limit) Effectively unbounded
Cost per query Prefill of whole corpus (cached prefix helps) Small prompt; retrieval infra cost
Latency High TTFT unless cached Low prompt, extra retrieval hop
Freshness Re-send or re-cache Update the index
Cross-doc reasoning Strong when it fits Weak if retrieval misses pieces
Access control Whole prompt visible to the model Filter before the prompt
Failure mode Context rot, lost in the middle Retrieval miss, bad chunking
Debuggability Hard to see what the model used Retrieved set is inspectable

Research (e.g. "Long Context vs. RAG for LLMs: An Evaluation and Revisits", 2025) finds long context often does better on Wikipedia-style or well-structured tasks while RAG holds up for dialogue or fragmented queries (verify details); the answer is task dependent, so measure.

Cost sketch: 100K-token corpus, 10K queries/day, $3 per 1M input (illustrative). Uncached: 10K x 100K = 1B tokens = $3,000/day. RAG with 6K prompts: 60M tokens = $180/day plus vector DB. With caching at a 90% discount (verify) long context is about $300/day plus cache writes, which changes the answer. That is why you compute, not assume.

Deep RAG design is C4; this question is the decision layer.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Declaring RAG dead because windows grew.
  • Ignoring per-user ACLs when stuffing everything in the prompt.
  • Comparing on a benchmark that doesn't resemble your queries.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is a hybrid? → Retrieve top-100 chunks, rerank, pass 20-30K tokens ordered by relevance.
  2. How does caching shift the break-even? → Makes static-corpus long context cheap; useless for rapidly changing or per-user corpora.
  3. How do you prove the choice? → A/B on a labelled query set, tracking accuracy, cost per query and p95 latency.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "long context for small data, RAG for big". Senior: tabulates axes, does the cost math with caching, raises ACLs and debuggability, and ends with a measured hybrid.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A legal-search team moved from RAG to full-document prompts for single-contract review (accuracy up) while keeping RAG for cross-portfolio search where documents number in the millions.

questions.contextHtml: An internal analyst assistant was upgraded to "use more context": retrieval top-k went from 8 to 60 chunks (about 4K to 38K tokens), reasoning that the new model has a 200K window (verify). Two weeks later, user thumbs-down rose from 6% to 14%. Offline eval on the 300-question set: accuracy 84% at k=8, 76% at k=60. Logs show answers citing wrong but plausible numbers from near-duplicate quarterly reports; latency p95 went from 2.1 s to 6.8 s; cost per query tripled. Retrieval recall@60 improved from 88% to 96%.
questions.promptHtml: Why did quality go down although recall went up, and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The model is hallucinating, add 'only use the context' to the prompt." Ignores that more context added distractors.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did anything else change (model version, chunking, prompt)? Are failures concentrated where near-duplicate chunks exist? Where is the gold chunk positioned in the 60? Is the order by relevance or by document?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll k back to 8-12 behind a flag while investigating.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) distractors: similar-looking quarterly reports confuse the model (context rot: performance degrades with length and with semantically similar distractors); (b) lost-in-the-middle: gold chunk sits mid-prompt; (c) order is by document id, not relevance; (d) conflicting numbers across chunks with no metadata (date) to disambiguate; (e) red herring: the new model version itself.
  4. How I'd verify each: Position sweep of gold chunk; ablation k in {8, 15, 30, 60} with fixed model; failure bucketing by "answer found in a distractor chunk"; check chunk headers for period/date; rerun with old model.
  5. Root cause: Recall is not the objective; precision of the final context is. Adding 52 mostly irrelevant, near-duplicate chunks raised the chance of the model choosing the wrong one, and diluted attention.
  6. Fix: Short term k=10-15 with a cross-encoder rerank; chunk metadata (report period, entity) injected into each chunk header; relevance ordering with best at start and end. Long term: query-aware filtering by period/entity before retrieval; dedupe; evaluate by k curve.
  7. Prevention: Eval gate on accuracy-by-k for any context-size change; log context tokens and distractor rate; dashboards of accuracy by input length.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't push recall further; don't blame the model without an A/B; reranking adds latency (tens of ms to low hundreds, verify) but lowers prefill cost.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Rerank hurts a few multi-hop questions? -> Use adaptive k: small by default, expand when the reranker scores are flat.
  • Users want longer answers with all sources? -> Summarize per source (map-reduce) rather than one big prompt.
  • Context rot reports say all models degrade? -> Yes, to differing degrees; measure your model.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team's accuracy curve versus k peaked at 12 and then slid for every model they tested; they shipped k=12 with a reranker and saved 70% of token cost.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: prompt tweaks only.
  • Hire: identifies distractors/order, rolls back, uses ablation.
  • Strong hire: distinguishes recall from context precision, adds metadata, rerank, eval gate, adaptive k.

questions.promptHtml: What is "context rot", why does performance degrade as input grows even on simple tasks, and what can you do about it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know long-context quality is non-uniform and can design around it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Context rot is the observed decline in model reliability as input length increases, even when the task stays the same difficulty. Chroma's 2025 study reported degradation across many models on controlled tasks, worsened by distractors that are semantically close to the answer and by lower similarity between question and needle (verify details in the report). Causes are not fully settled: attention dilution, positional biases and training distribution on shorter sequences. I manage it by keeping context small and relevant.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Mechanisms (hypotheses):

  1. Softmax dilution: attention weights sum to 1. With n tokens, the signal on the relevant ones competes with n-1 others; irrelevant but plausible tokens collect mass.
  2. Positional bias: primacy/recency (Q132) and weaker training signal at long positions; most pretraining data is short.
  3. Distractors: hard negatives that look like the answer (near-duplicate reports) are far worse than random filler.
  4. Task type: retrieval of a salient fact degrades slowly; reasoning or aggregation degrades fast (RULER).
  5. Extension method: models stretched with RoPE scaling can lose precision (Q131).

Implication: capacity grows faster than reliability, so each token you add has a cost in expected accuracy as well as in dollars.

Mitigations: retrieve then rerank, shrink to what's needed; structure and label content; put instructions and question at the edges; summarise or compact old turns; split tasks (map-reduce) into smaller calls; keep tool outputs concise; evaluate accuracy vs length for your task.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def accuracy_by_length(cases, model, lengths=(4_000, 16_000, 64_000, 128_000)):
    out = {}
    for L in lengths:
        ok = [model(c.build(L)) == c.gold for c in cases]
        out[L] = sum(ok) / len(ok)
    return out    # plot; pick the context size where the curve bends

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Quoting the advertised window as the safe operating point.
  • Padding prompts with "just in case" content.
  • Treating a single benchmark as universal.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How is it different from lost in the middle? → That is position-dependent; rot is length- and distractor-dependent. They compound.
  2. Does a bigger model fix it? → Reduces, not eliminates; measure.
  3. How do you detect it in prod? → Slice quality metrics by prompt token buckets.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "long prompts are less accurate". Senior: separates mechanisms, stresses distractors, offers measurable mitigations and treats context as a budgeted resource.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A coding agent's success rate dropped steadily after about 60K tokens of accumulated tool logs; compaction at 40K restored it.

questions.contextHtml: A legal-tech startup reviews M&A data rooms. A deal has 400-900 documents, about 1.5-4M tokens in total; analysts ask 30-60 questions per deal over a week ("list all change-of-control clauses", "any contradictions on liability caps?"). Acceptance: recall of clauses above 95%, every claim cited to page, no cross-client leakage. Budget: $40 per deal in LLM spend. Illustrative price $3 per 1M input, cached reads at 10% (verify). Largest available window is 1M tokens (verify).

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Stuff everything into the 1M window" (does not fit, 95% recall unlikely) or "plain top-5 RAG" (misses exhaustive-list questions).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What fraction of questions are exhaustive ("all clauses") vs pointed? Are documents stable during the deal? Is page-level citation mandatory? How is recall measured and on what labelled set? Is customer data allowed to leave the region?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (design). I'd first build a labelled set of 100 questions from two past deals.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) exhaustive questions need map-reduce over every document, since retrieval top-k cannot guarantee coverage; (b) pointed questions suit retrieval; (c) 4M tokens cannot fit one window, and 1M-token prompts risk rot; (d) cost: one full-corpus pass is about 4M x $3/1M = $12, so 3 passes already bust the budget unless cached.
  4. How I'd verify each: Measure recall for retrieval-only, map-reduce, and 1M-window on the labelled set; count tokens per strategy; test cache hit behaviour and TTL; position and length ablations.
  5. Design: Per-document extraction pass once at ingest (map): for each doc (cap 20-50K tokens per call) extract structured clause records with page citations and store them. Exhaustive questions query the structured store plus targeted verification; pointed questions use hybrid retrieval then 20-40K token context. Cross-document contradictions: retrieve candidate pairs from extracted records, then put only those clauses side by side in a small prompt. Tenant isolation: per-deal index and per-deal credentials; no shared cache across tenants.
  6. Fix/costing: Ingest map pass 4M tokens x $3/1M = $12 once, plus output; queries mostly under 40K tokens: 50 queries x 40K = 2M tokens = $6. Total about $20, under $40.
  7. Prevention: Regression eval per prompt/model change; recall by question type; audit citation validity automatically (page text contains the quote).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not rely on one giant prompt; extraction misses compound across stages, so spot-check and keep source text for verification; indexing latency before first query.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Documents change daily? -> Incremental re-extraction keyed by content hash.
  • A new model has a 10M window? -> Re-run the eval; rot and cost may still favour the structured approach.
  • Client forbids third-party embeddings? -> Self-hosted embedding model or lexical retrieval plus extraction.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A first version used top-8 retrieval for "find all indemnity caps" and silently missed 11 of 40; per-document extraction made coverage a property of the pipeline, not of a similarity threshold.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: all-in window or top-k only.
  • Hire: recognizes exhaustive vs pointed questions and costs it.
  • Strong hire: map-reduce design, tenancy, cited verification, eval and budget math.

questions.promptHtml: A conversation or agent run will exceed the window. What are your options for managing context, and how do you choose?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks practical toolbox and trade-off awareness for long-running chat and agents.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Five options: truncate (drop oldest), sliding window, summarize older content, retrieve relevant memory on demand, and offload to external state such as files or notes. I combine them: pin instructions, keep the last N turns verbatim, summarize the middle, and store facts and artifacts externally with retrieval. Choice depends on whether old details are needed verbatim, cost of an extra summarization call, and error tolerance.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Strategy Keeps Loses Cost
Truncate oldest Recent turns Early facts, instructions if unpinned Free
Sliding window + pins Recent plus system Mid-history Free
Rolling summary Gist Exact values, quotes 1 extra call per compaction
Retrieval memory Relevant old items Order and nuance Index + retrieval
External scratchpad/files Exact artifacts Needs model to re-read Tool calls
Tool-result clearing Decisions Raw tool output Free

Practical rules:

  • Compact at a threshold (e.g. 70% of window) rather than at overflow.
  • Keep exact identifiers, numbers, decisions and open TODOs in the summary; use a structured summary schema.
  • Summaries drift when summarised repeatedly; re-derive from raw logs periodically if retained.
  • Cache-friendly: append-only history preserves the cached prefix; editing earlier content invalidates caching. Agent-specific memory design belongs to C5.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def compact(messages, count, summarize, window=128_000, trigger=0.7, keep_last=8):
    if sum(count(m["content"]) for m in messages) < trigger * window:
        return messages
    system = [m for m in messages if m["role"] == "system"]
    rest = [m for m in messages if m["role"] != "system"]
    old, recent = rest[:-keep_last], rest[-keep_last:]
    summary = summarize(old)   # structured: facts, decisions, open items
    return system + [{"role": "user", "content": f"Summary of earlier turns:\n{summary}"}] + recent

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Summarizing away exact numbers or user constraints.
  • Compacting at 99% so the summary call itself overflows.
  • Rewriting history each turn and destroying prompt-cache hits.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you evaluate a summary? → Question-answering over held-out facts from the original versus from the summary.
  2. When prefer retrieval memory? → Many independent facts, rarely needed together.
  3. Does compaction affect cost? → Lowers per-turn tokens but costs a call; amortised over later turns.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "summarize old messages". Senior: tiered strategy, structured summary, thresholds, drift, and cache interaction.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An agent that summarized every 10 turns lost a user-stated constraint ("never touch prod DB"); pinning constraints in a separate non-summarized block fixed it.

questions.contextHtml: A document-chat product has 20K DAU, each session uploads a 90K-token document and asks about 8 questions. Today the full document plus history is sent every turn with no caching: 20K x 8 x about 92K = 14.7B input tokens/day. Illustrative $3 per 1M input => $44K/day. Marketing plans a 10x user push. On a self-hosted fallback with an 8B model, you saw 16 GiB KV per 128K request and OOMs when concurrency exceeded 3 per GPU. p95 TTFT is 11 s.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do before the 10x traffic arrives?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add GPUs / negotiate a discount." Ignores that 7 of 8 turns recompute the same document.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the document identical across turns of a session (yes)? Cache TTL options? Are questions localized to part of the document? Latency vs accuracy priorities? Do users re-ask across sessions on the same document?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Enable provider prompt caching: document first, history appended after, question last. Keep the prefix byte-stable.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) repeated prefill of the identical 90K document is the dominant cost; (b) TTL (minutes) may expire between slow user turns; (c) some questions only need a section; (d) the self-hosted path needs admission control.
  4. How I'd verify each: Measure cache hit rate and inter-turn gaps from logs; compute spend: with 7 of 8 turns hitting cache at 10% price (verify), input = 20K x (1 x 90K x 1.25 write premium + 7 x 90K x 0.1 + ~8 x 2K) = about 20K x (112K + 63K + 16K) = 3.8B equivalent tokens => about $11K/day, a 74% cut. Check the p95 TTFT on cache hits.
  5. Root cause: Stateless API usage pattern repeating identical prefill.
  6. Fix: Caching (with keep-alive if TTL is short and economics justify); route simple factual questions to retrieved sections (6-10K tokens) with a smaller model; cap history via compaction; for self-hosting use prefix caching, KV quantization (fp8), chunked prefill and admission control on estimated KV bytes, and autoscale on queue depth.
  7. Prevention: Dashboards: cache hit rate, tokens/session, cost/session, TTFT by prompt-size bucket; budget alerts; load test with long documents.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Cache writes cost a premium (verify), so single-turn sessions can get more expensive; don't evict by TTL alone; retrieval routing risks quality, so gate by eval.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Same document reused by many users? -> Share a document-level cache only if tenancy and ACLs allow; otherwise per-user.
  • Hit rate stuck at 40%? -> Look for timestamps, per-user IDs or reordered tool schemas in the prefix.
  • GPU bill still high? -> Reduce bytes per token: GQA models, fp8 KV, shorter windows by section routing.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: One team's cache hit rate was 0% for a month because the SDK serialized tool definitions in nondeterministic order; sorting keys fixed it and cut spend by two thirds.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scale hardware or discount.
  • Hire: caching with token math.
  • Strong hire: cache pitfalls, routing by eval, KV and admission control, monitoring.

questions.contextHtml: You run a contract-summary service on a 32K-window model with chunk-and-merge (map-reduce) summarization at 15K requests/day. A vendor's newer model offers 200K (verify) at a similar per-token price. Product wants to drop map-reduce and send whole documents (average 70K tokens, p95 160K) in one call. Current eval: faithfulness 91%, key-clause coverage 88%. Latency p95 now 9 s; a pilot on the new model gave p95 31 s on the long tail and coverage 90% on average but 79% for documents above 120K tokens.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Switch everything; it scored higher on average." Averages hide the long-tail regression and latency breach.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the latency SLO and is summarization sync or async? What is the size distribution of documents? Does the new model change the output format or tokenizer (tokens per document differ across vendors)? What is the rollback cost?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Keep production on the current path; shadow-run the new path on a sample, no user impact.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) coverage drop above 120K is context rot / lost in the middle; (b) latency tail comes from prefill of 120K+ tokens; (c) tokenizer difference makes the real token count larger than estimated; (d) average improvement is driven by mid-sized documents where whole-document context helps.
  4. How I'd verify each: Bucket eval by length (0-30K, 30-70K, 70-120K, 120K+); position-sweep key clauses; recount tokens with the new tokenizer; check TTFT vs length.
  5. Root cause: Long-context quality is not uniform; one model change mixes two variables (model, context strategy).
  6. Fix (staged): Length-based routing: single-call for docs up to about 100K (where eval shows gains), map-reduce for longer, perhaps with larger chunks (e.g. 60K) than before. Canary 5% -> 25% -> 100% with automatic rollback on coverage, faithfulness, p95 latency and cost guardrails. Make summarization async for long docs if the SLO allows.
  7. Prevention: Keep both pipelines runnable for a deprecation window; eval gates per length bucket; alert on tokens per request drift.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't change model and strategy in the same step if I can separate them (test new model with old map-reduce first); don't delete the old path; routing adds complexity but protects the tail.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Vendor deprecates the old model in 60 days? -> Time-box: prioritize the model swap with old strategy, then optimize strategy.
  • Cost per doc goes up 20% on 70K docs? -> Compare against saved map-reduce overhead and quality gain; decide with unit economics.
  • Eval set is too small for the 120K bucket? -> Mine more long documents or synthesize by concatenation with care; widen confidence intervals before deciding.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A swap that looked 2 points better on average silently lost 9 points on the longest 8% of documents, which were the highest-value customers; per-bucket gating caught it before full rollout.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: switch based on the average.
  • Hire: canary and length-bucketed eval.
  • Strong hire: separates variables, length routing, rollback guardrails, tokenizer and latency checks.
